summary: This document specifies how BGP can advertise that a router has bound an MPLS label, or a sequence of labels, to an address prefix. The information is carried in a BGP UPDATE message, which lets labeled paths be set up across networks using BGP.

plainLanguage.summary: BGP usually tells routers where to go. This also lets it tell them what sticker to put on the packet to get there.

questions: how does bgp distribute mpls labels
how does bgp carry mpls labels
what is the multiple labels capability
subtitle: How BGP can announce not just a route to a prefix, but the MPLS label or labels bound to it.

tldr.problem: RFC 3107 let BGP carry MPLS labels with prefixes, but it left label sequences, withdrawals and the interaction with ordinary routes unclear, and implementations disagreed.
tldr.mechanism: A BGP UPDATE with an MP_REACH_NLRI attribute carries the prefix and its label(s) in the NLRI, with the next hop naming the node that bound them. A new Multiple Labels Capability must be exchanged before more than one label may be sent.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8277 obsoletes RFC 3107, removes an unimplemented feature, and fixes the encodings and withdrawal rules while staying interoperable with deployed RFC 3107 code.

today: RFC 8277 is a Proposed Standard from October 2017 and obsoletes RFC 3107. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why RFC 3107 Needed Replacing
sections.content:
RFC 3107 defined how a router can use BGP to say it has bound an MPLS label, or a sequence of labels forming part of a label stack, to an address prefix. The UPDATE message carries the prefix and the label(s) in its Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI) field, and its Next Hop field names the node where the prefix is bound to those labels. Each such UPDATE also advertises a path to the prefix.

RFC 8277 lists the problems that got in the way of interoperability. RFC 3107 did not define what a sequence of labels means, and many implementations assumed only one label. Its withdrawal rules were unclear, and its optional "Advertising Multiple Routes to a Destination" feature was never implemented as specified. It was silent on how an UPDATE with labels interacts with one without, and it never mentioned VPN-IPv4 and VPN-IPv6.

This document replaces RFC 3107. It adds a new BGP Capability for label sequences, drops the unimplemented feature in favor of the procedures of RFC 7911, and declares most label and no-label interactions to be local policy for backwards compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rulebook was fuzzy, so different routers played by different rules and sometimes could not understand each other. This new rulebook cleans that up without breaking the old games.

sections.title: Binding a Prefix to Labels in BGP
sections.content:
To advertise a binding, node N sends a Multiprotocol BGP UPDATE with an MP_REACH_NLRI attribute, as in RFC 4760. The Network Address of Next Hop field holds an IP address of N, and the labels and prefix are encoded in the NLRI.

The address family fields say what kind of prefix it is. For an IPv4 or VPN-IPv4 prefix the AFI is 1, and for an IPv6 or VPN-IPv6 prefix the AFI is 2. For a plain IPv4 or IPv6 prefix the SAFI is 4, and for a VPN-IPv4 or VPN-IPv6 prefix the SAFI is 128. Other AFI values with SAFI 4 or 128 are out of scope.

The document calls a message with SAFI x a "SAFI-x UPDATE". It also says this is not the only way to use BGP to advertise label bindings, citing other mechanisms in other RFCs, and it does not discuss which to use when.
sections.plainLanguage: A router sends a note that says "for this address, use sticker number so-and-so, and send it to me." Small codes in the note say which kind of address it is.

sections.title: The Multiple Labels Capability
sections.content:
Sending more than one label per prefix is gated by a new BGP capability. IANA assigned Capability Code 8 to the Multiple Labels Capability, which is carried in the BGP OPEN message. Its value is one or more four-octet triples: a two-octet AFI, a one-octet SAFI and a one-octet Count. The Count is the maximum number of labels the sender can process in a received UPDATE of that AFI/SAFI, and 255 means no limit.

Unless both speakers on a session send the capability, every SAFI-4 or SAFI-128 UPDATE must bind a prefix to a single label and use the single-label encoding. An implementation that sends the capability MUST be able to support at least two labels in the NLRI. Triples with a Count of 0 or 1 MUST NOT be sent and are ignored if received, and if a capability contains several triples for the same AFI/SAFI, all but the first are ignored. A capability whose length is not a multiple of four is malformed.

A speaker SHOULD NOT send more labels than its peer announced. If it receives more than it announced, it must apply the "treat-as-withdraw" strategy of RFC 7606. There is also a space limit: the NLRI length is limited to 255 bits including the prefix, so only so many labels fit.

The document also covers graceful restart. If the capability was exchanged before a restart but not after, or the Count was reduced, prefixes advertised with too many labels MUST be explicitly withdrawn.
sections.plainLanguage: Before anyone puts two stickers on a package, both sides have to say "I can read that." If they do not both say it, everyone sticks to one sticker.

sections.title: NLRI Encodings and Withdrawals
sections.content:
Without the capability, the NLRI holds a one-octet Length (in bits), a 20-bit Label, a 3-bit Rsrv field and a 1-bit S field, then the prefix. Rsrv SHOULD be zero on transmission and is ignored on reception. S MUST be one on transmission and is ignored on reception. Length is 20 plus 3 plus 1 plus the prefix length in bits.

With the capability exchanged, the NLRI carries a run of labels, each 24 bits wide, followed by the prefix. The S bit MUST be 0 in every label except the last, where it MUST be 1. Failing to set S in the last label makes the NLRI impossible to parse. If the procedures of RFC 7911 are in use, a four-octet path identifier comes before the Length field.

To withdraw a binding, a speaker sends an MP_UNREACH_NLRI attribute. Its NLRI is a Length, a three-octet Compatibility field and the prefix. The Compatibility field SHOULD be set to 0x800000 on transmission, but its value MUST be ignored on reception, because some implementations send 0x000000. The withdrawal works whether or not the capability was used. It removes both the label binding and the path to the prefix that was advertised in that SAFI.
sections.plainLanguage: Each sticker is a little numbered tag, and the last one is marked "this is the final one" so the reader knows where the address starts. To cancel a message, you send a short note naming the same address.

sections.title: Changing, Comparing and Propagating Routes
sections.content:
If a speaker receives a new UPDATE for the same prefix and next hop on the same session with different labels, and RFC 7911 is not in use, the new UPDATE implicitly withdraws the old one. With RFC 7911, the same path identifier means replacement, while a different identifier means both bindings stay, and the speaker may load-balance between them using the labels from each. Hearing the same prefix and next hop with a different label on a different session suggests at least two paths, and the speaker MAY load-balance.

Two SAFI-4 routes for the same prefix, received on different sessions or with different path identifiers, MUST be considered comparable even if their labels differ. The BGP best-path selection of RFC 4271 then applies, and without RFC 7911 only the best path is propagated. The same holds for SAFI-128.

When propagating, if the next hop is unchanged the labels MUST be unchanged. If the next hop is changed, the labels MUST be those bound at the new next hop, and local policy may replace one label by one, one by many, many by one or many by many. A route MUST NOT be sent to a peer that did not negotiate multiple labels, or that announced a smaller limit, and any earlier version with fewer labels MUST be withdrawn from that peer.
sections.plainLanguage: If two messages give different stickers for the same address, the router keeps the newer one, or in special cases keeps both and takes turns. When it passes a message along, it makes sure the next router can read the stickers.

sections.title: Data Plane and SAFI-1 Relationship
sections.content:
The data plane section explains what a router does with packets. A speaker S1 that received label L1 from next hop N1, and advertised label L2 with itself as next hop, swaps L2 for L1 and tunnels the packet to N1. Tunnels might be an LSP, a Layer 2 adjacency, or IP, GRE or UDP tunnels. If S1 received a sequence of k labels and advertised one, it pops L2 and pushes the whole sequence so the first label ends up on top. S1 may also advertise several labels, for example when it uses context labels, which are known only to S1.

The RFC warns that replacing labels with sequences must be done carefully, because the next hop can receive an unexpected combined label stack. TTL and Traffic Class values for pushed labels are left to local policy, as are the rules for whether SAFI-4 routes may forward IP packets.

A speaker may also hold both a SAFI-1 and a SAFI-4 route for the same prefix. Implementations differ: some keep them independent, some treat them as comparable, some allow both on one session, and a speaker MAY convert a SAFI-4 route to SAFI-1 when propagating to a session without SAFI-4. All of these are local policy, and the RFC says they may cause unexpected behavior or lack of interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: When a package arrives with a sticker, the router swaps it for the right one and sends it on through a tunnel. Different routers handle plain and sticker-labeled addresses in their own ways, so results can differ.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
IANA assigned value 8 for the Multiple Labels Capability in the BGP "Capability Codes" registry. It also marked value 4 ("Multiple routes to a destination capability") as deprecated, and updated the references for SAFI 4 and SAFI 128 to this document.

The security considerations of BGP in RFC 4271 apply. A non-conforming implementation that sends multiple labels without exchanging the capability will likely cause a conforming one to reset the session. The tunneled packets need encapsulation, and the RFC does not choose one. If the encapsulation lacks integrity and authentication, including the MPLS encapsulation most commonly used, a label stack could be altered in flight, causing misdelivery.

Label bindings may be learned by routers that were not meant to know them if BGP sessions do not provide privacy. The RFC also suggests that a speaker distinguish internal from external interfaces and avoid advertising the same labels on both, so packets with spoofed labels from untrusted sources can be discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: If the sticker on a package can be changed on the way, it might go to the wrong house. So routers should only trust stickers that came from the right side of the building.

fields.desc: SHOULD be zero on transmission; ignored on reception.

fields.desc: MUST be one on transmission; ignored on reception.
